items.topic: Async job persistence backend for video jobs
items.context: Video jobs are async and long-running (minutes). The job system needs to persist state across restarts and support status polling. Options range from in-memory (simplest, loses state on restart) to SQLite (durable, single-node) to PostgreSQL (shared resource, already available in Vrooli).

options.label: SQLite — embedded, durable, zero-config, sufficient for single-node
options.rationale: Video Studio runs on a single server. SQLite handles concurrent reads well, and WAL mode supports the polling pattern. No external dependency. Keeps the scenario self-contained.

options.label: PostgreSQL via Vrooli resource — shared, scalable, familiar
options.rationale: Vrooli already has PostgreSQL as a shared resource. Enables cross-scenario queries (e.g., marketing crew checking job status). But adds a resource dependency and schema migration overhead for a single-scenario job table.

options.label: File-based JSON — jobs stored as JSON files in a jobs/ directory
options.rationale: Simplest to implement, naturally browsable, but poor concurrent access and no query capability. Could work for low-volume P0.

options.label: Other
options.rationale: Provide your own approach

items.topic: Xvfb display allocation strategy for concurrent desktop recordings
items.context: S2D hardcodes display :99. Video Studio may run multiple desktop recordings concurrently (e.g., multi-scene video with parallel segment capture). Display collisions would cause recording failures or cross-contamination.

options.label: Dynamic allocation with lock files — find next free display (:99, :100, ...) using /tmp/.X{n}-lock
options.rationale: Standard X11 pattern. Xvfb itself checks for lock files. Wrap in a helper that scans for the first unlocked display number. Proven, no external deps.

options.label: Fixed pool — pre-allocate displays :99-:103 (5 concurrent max) with a semaphore
options.rationale: Simpler to reason about. Bounded concurrency prevents resource exhaustion. But arbitrary limit may be too low or wasteful.

options.label: One display, sequential recording — queue desktop recordings and run one at a time
options.rationale: Simplest implementation. Desktop recording concurrency may not be a P0 requirement. Limits throughput but avoids all display management complexity.

options.label: Other
options.rationale: Provide your own approach

items.topic: BAS API stability — how to handle potential API changes
items.context: BAS's HTTP API was designed for its own UI, not as a stable external contract. Video Studio will depend on specific endpoints (start recording, get status, download artifact). If BAS API changes, Video Studio breaks silently. Need a strategy to manage this coupling.

options.label: Version-pinned client with integration tests — BAS client targets a specific API version, integration tests run against live BAS to detect drift
options.rationale: Practical approach: document which BAS endpoints are used, pin expected response shapes, and let CI catch breakage. Doesn't require BAS changes.

options.label: Formal BAS API contract — add OpenAPI spec to BAS, Video Studio generates client from spec
options.rationale: Gold standard for inter-scenario dependencies. But requires BAS to adopt OpenAPI, which is out of Video Studio's scope and adds cross-scenario coordination overhead.

options.label: Adapter/anti-corruption layer — Video Studio defines its own recording interface, thin adapter translates to BAS API
options.rationale: Isolates Video Studio from BAS API details. Easy to swap recording backends later. But adds a layer of indirection for P0.

options.label: Other
options.rationale: Provide your own approach

items.freeform: Use existing proto contract with ‘discovery’ package setup that’s done for reliable cross-scenario communication in existing scenarios

items.topic: P0 compositing scope — how much FFmpeg compositing to support initially
items.context: FFmpeg compositing can range from simple concatenation to complex filter graphs with crossfades, picture-in-picture, audio mixing, and effects. More capability means more complexity and more ways things can fail. P0 needs a clear line.

options.label: Concat only — join segments sequentially with consistent encoding, no transitions
options.rationale: Dead simple FFmpeg concat demuxer. Reliable, fast, easy to test. Good enough for demo videos where scenes play back-to-back. Transitions can be added in P1.

options.label: Concat + crossfade transitions — add 0.5-1s crossfade between segments
options.rationale: Noticeably more polished output. FFmpeg's xfade filter handles this, but requires precise duration math and re-encoding. Moderate complexity increase.

options.label: Full filter graph — concat, crossfade, text overlays, audio mixing
options.rationale: Professional-quality output from day one. But FFmpeg filter graphs are fragile, hard to debug, and significantly increase development/testing time for P0.

options.label: Other
options.rationale: Provide your own approach

items.context: The AI scripting agent converts a text brief into a structured recording script. LLMs can produce invalid JSON, hallucinate non-existent URLs, or generate impractical action sequences (e.g., 'click the buy button' when there is no buy button). The system needs a strategy for handling these failures gracefully.

options.label: Schema validation + single retry with error feedback — validate script against JSON schema, if invalid retry once with the validation error in context
options.rationale: Balances reliability with simplicity. One retry with error context usually fixes structural issues. Fail the job if the retry also fails. Keeps P0 implementation simple.

options.label: Schema validation + escalation — validate, fail the job on invalid script, surface the error for human review
options.rationale: Simplest implementation. No retry logic. Human sees the failed brief and can rephrase or debug. But reduces autonomy.

options.label: Multi-step validation — schema check → dry-run simulation → record, with retries at each step
options.rationale: Most robust. Dry-run catches impractical actions before wasting recording time. But significantly more complex and requires building a simulation layer.

options.label: Other
options.rationale: Provide your own approach
